![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/2d6dc14c5296291bffa9a942ef9465b27477ee4c58550faba507703c2781a54b.png)

A thin sheet of caramel occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves $x=1,y=x$ and $y=2,$ as shown above. The mass density function $\lambda $ of the sheet is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{y}{x}.$ Find the total mass of the caramel sheet.
worked_solution:
The mass of the caramel sheet occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{y}{x}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region. 

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So the $x$-limits are $1\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/281ea7be1ef48c149bb4bcfd09aa41357caa8bb28adfc48285d298fb3cf89f3c.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y):1\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{x}^{2}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x}[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{{2}^{2}}{4})-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\frac{{1}^{2}}{4}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the ice sheet is $M=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{3}{4}.$
